title: Cross-Platform
description: Cross-Platform is the 2010 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of electronic rock about building software for the web, phones, games and tiny embedded devices. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword plays lead guitar, Wyrd drives everything with arpeggiated synths and beats, and Bytes plays drums and electronic pads and sings backup. Clients and servers, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, responsive design, web APIs, the app lifecycle, touch input, battery life, the game loop, entity component systems, embedded systems and the internet of things. Released first as an app. Qword’s solos didn’t fit on a phone screen, and Wyrd made a version that runs on a smart fridge. Play loud. Charge first.
tagline: The 2010 electronic rock album from Procedural Byts: a platforms course in twelve songs, released as an app and playable on a fridge.
lineup: The four-piece, on every platform. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays lead guitar. Wyrd plays arpeggiated synths and electronic beats. Bytes plays live drums with electronic pads and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the member who insisted the app pick up exactly where it left off after every phone call. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits, with solos too wide for a phone. Qword now plays a compact version for small screens and refuses to call it shorter.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, on arpeggiated synths and beats, and the builder of the album app, the catch-the-duck game and the fridge version.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, live drums plus electronic pads, backing vocals, and the one who wanted a game in the app in the first place.

members.name: Null
members.bio: An entity with a position, a sprite and a velocity. No sound component.

story.heading: Released as an App
paragraphs: By 2010, everyone had a phone in their pocket, so the band decided to release the album first as an app. It worked on one kind of phone. Then they made it work on the other kind. Then on the web. Then on tablets, which nobody had planned for.

Qword’s solos didn’t fit on a phone screen. The app scrolled sideways during the long ones, and fans kept pausing them by accident with their thumbs. Qword now plays a compact version for small screens and refuses to call it shorter.

The first version of the app kept the GPS switched on so it could show you the nearest record store. It drained a full battery in an hour. The fix became Battery Low. Getting the app to pick up exactly where it left off after a phone call took another month, and became Background.

Bytes wanted a game in the app, so Wyrd built one: catch the duck. Every object in it was an entity made of components. Null got a position, a sprite and a velocity, but no sound component. Nobody added one. Nobody needed to.
Then Wyrd made a version that runs on a smart fridge, in sixty-four kilobytes of memory. It plays the album whenever you open the door. It is, by a wide margin, the most-played version.
After the four-rooms recording of 2001, the band recorded this one the old way: all four in one room, on one platform. Everyone agreed it was a relief.

cover_sub: The 2010 album. Released as an app. Also runs on a fridge.

songs.title: Cross-Platform

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: One phone in my pocket and another one in yours,
A laptop and a tablet and a screen beside the doors.
Every platform has its rules, its language and its store,
Write it once for all of them, then fix it four times more!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Cross-platform! (Everywhere at once!)
Cross-platform! (Every screen, every one!)
Native for the speed or the web for the reach,
Cross-platform, cross-platform, a little bit of each!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Native code is fast and fits the feel of every phone,
But you write it twice, or three times, every platform on its own.
The web runs everywhere, a browser’s all you need,
A framework in between, and you pay a little speed!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Native! (Fast!) Web! (Everywhere!)
Hybrid! (Somewhere in between, but there!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays the same arpeggio four times through four different synths, one per platform. It’s recognizably the same tune every time, but each version has to be adjusted to sound right on that synth.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Cross-platform! (Everywhere at once!)
Cross-platform! (Every screen, every one!)
Native for the speed or the web for the reach,
Cross-platform, cross-platform, a little bit of each!

songs.note: The album was released on four platforms at once. On the first day, it worked on three of them.
songs.lesson: Software runs on many platforms, like the web, phones, tablets, desktops, game consoles and tiny embedded devices, each with its own languages, rules and app stores. Native apps are fast and feel right on their platform but have to be written separately for each one. Web apps run anywhere there’s a browser. Cross-platform frameworks share most of the code, at some cost in speed or polish.

songs.title: Client and Server

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I type in the address and I press the key,
The browser sends a request across the sea.
The server finds the page and sends it right back down,
Request and response, all the way around!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Client! (I ask!)
Server! (I answer!)
Request and response, over and over again,
Client and server, server and client, and the web begins!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The client is the browser running on your machine,
The server’s in a building that you’ve never seen.
HTTP’s the language, GET to read and POST to send,
A status code comes back to tell you how it ends!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Two hundred! (Okay!) Four oh four! (Not found!)
Five hundred! (Server error!) And it all comes back around!

parts.label: Request and response: Qword and Nyble
parts.desc: Qword plays a question, Nyble answers it, and Qword never plays the next question until the answer has arrived. Once, Nyble answers with a single sour note: four oh four.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Client! (I ask!)
Server! (I answer!)
Request and response, over and over again,
Client and server, server and client, and the web begins!

songs.note: Every fan who downloaded the app sent a request to the band’s server. On release day, it got four oh fours for an hour.
songs.lesson: The web runs on a client-server model: a client, usually a browser, sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server sends back a response. GET asks for something and POST sends data. Every response carries a status code: 200 means OK, 404 means not found, and 500 means something broke on the server.

songs.title: Structure, Style, Behavior

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: HTML’s the skeleton, the headings and the text,

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: JavaScript’s the muscle, and it makes the page move,
Click a button and it answers, it updates in the groove.
Keep the three apart, each language does its part,

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Tags! (The bones!) Rules! (The skin!)

parts.label: Three layers: full band
parts.desc: The solo is built in three passes: Nyble plays the bare riff (structure), Wyrd dresses it in synth tone and effects (style), and Bytes makes it move with changing rhythms (behavior). Take any layer away and the other two still stand.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Structure! (HTML!)
Style! (CSS!)
Behavior! (JavaScript!)
Three layers, and the page is dressed!

songs.note: Recorded in three passes: first the bones, then the clothes, then the moves.
songs.lesson: Web pages separate three jobs. HTML gives the page its structure and meaning: headings, paragraphs, links. CSS controls how it looks: colors, fonts, layout. JavaScript adds behavior: responding to clicks and updating the page. Keeping the three apart makes pages easier to change and more accessible.

songs.title: Responsive

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: On a wide screen I spread out in three columns side by side,
On a phone I stack in one, and nothing has to hide.
Same page, a different shape, it bends to fit the view,
The layout listens to the screen and knows just what to do!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Responsive! (Fit the screen!)
Responsive! (Every size between!)
Flexible grids and images that never overflow,
Responsive, responsive, wherever you go!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Start with the smallest screen, then add as there is room,
Mobile first, the essentials, then let the extras bloom.
Media queries ask how wide and change the rules to match,
Relative sizes, no fixed widths, no sideways scroll to catch!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Phone! (One column!) Tablet! (Two!)
Desktop! (Three!) The fridge! (Just the duck for you!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays the solo twice: a wide, sprawling version for a big stage, and a compact version for a small room that keeps every important note and drops the rest. Same solo, different screen.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Responsive! (Fit the screen!)
Responsive! (Every size between!)
Flexible grids and images that never overflow,
Responsive, responsive, wherever you go!

songs.note: The band’s website was rebuilt for this album to fit every screen. On the fridge, it shows only the duck.
songs.lesson: Responsive web design makes one page adapt to any screen size using flexible grids, images that scale, and CSS media queries that change the layout at different widths. Ethan Marcotte named the approach in 2010. Mobile-first design starts with the smallest screen and the essentials, then adds more layout as the screen gets bigger.

songs.title: Stateless

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Every request stands alone and brings everything it needs,
The server keeps no memory of yesterday’s deeds.
A resource has an address, and the verbs are all the same,
Get it, put it, post it, delete it by its name!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Stateless! (I don’t remember you!)
Stateless! (Tell me what to do!)
Resources and addresses and the same four verbs for all,
Stateless, stateless, and the servers stand tall!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: An API’s a promise between programs on the line,
Send me JSON and I’ll send some back, and everything is fine.
Stateless means a thousand servers can answer any call,
Scale it out across the world, and none of them will stall!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: GET! (Read it!) POST! (Make it!)
PUT! (Change it!) DELETE! (Take it!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Every fill Bytes plays is complete on its own: it doesn’t depend on the last one, and the next one doesn’t need to remember it. All four could be played in any order and still make sense.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Stateless! (I don’t remember you!)
Stateless! (Tell me what to do!)
Resources and addresses and the same four verbs for all,
Stateless, stateless, and the servers stand tall!

songs.note: The album app talked to the band’s server through a web API. The server never remembered anyone. That’s why it survived release day, eventually.
songs.lesson: Web APIs let programs talk to each other over HTTP. In the REST style (Roy Fielding, 2000), data is modeled as resources with addresses, changed with the same few methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), usually exchanging JSON. Each request is stateless: it carries everything the server needs, so any server can answer it, which makes it easy to add more servers.

songs.title: Background

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I’m playing on the screen and then the phone begins to ring,
I’m pushed into the background and I can’t do anything.
The system needs the memory, it might shut me down for good,
So save my place before it does, the way a good app should!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Background! (Paused, not gone!)
Background! (Save it and move on!)
Created, started, running, paused, then stopped and maybe killed,
Save it when you’re paused, and come back with nothing spilled!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The phone decides my life, not me, it starts me and it ends,
On a tiny battery and the memory it lends.
When the user comes back to me, they shouldn’t lose a thing,
Restore the screen exactly, like I never heard it ring!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Pause! (Save!) Resume! (Restore!)
Killed in the background! (Like I was there before!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s solo is interrupted four times by a ringing phone sample. Each time the band drops out, and each time Qword comes back on exactly the next note, as if nothing happened.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Background! (Paused, not gone!)
Background! (Save it and move on!)
Created, started, running, paused, then stopped and maybe killed,
Save it when you’re paused, and come back with nothing spilled!

songs.note: The app version of the album paused every time a fan’s phone rang, and always picked up exactly where it left off. That took a month to get right.
songs.lesson: On a phone, the operating system controls an app’s life. Apps get created, started, resumed, paused when they go into the background, stopped, and may be killed without warning when the phone needs memory. An app has to save its state when it’s paused and restore it when the user comes back, so nobody ever loses their place.

songs.title: Fat Finger

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: No mouse, no cursor, just a finger on the glass,
The finger’s bigger than the pixel and the buttons go too fast.
Make the targets big enough for a thumb to hit,
Leave a little space between them, and that’s it!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Fat finger! (Tap it!)
Fat finger! (Swipe it!)
Pinch to zoom and drag to move and hold to see some more,
Fat finger, fat finger, on the touchscreen floor!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: There’s no hover on a touchscreen, no tooltip in the air,
The finger hides the thing it’s touching, so show the feedback there.
Swipe and pinch and long press, gestures nobody can see,
Make them discoverable, or nobody finds the key!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Tap! (Select!) Swipe! (Next!)
Pinch! (Zoom!) Hold! (More!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays the solo on a touchscreen synth with no keys: swipes for slides, pinches for filter sweeps, a long press for a held chord. It sounds like gestures.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Fat finger! (Tap it!)
Fat finger! (Swipe it!)
Pinch to zoom and drag to move and hold to see some more,
Fat finger, fat finger, on the touchscreen floor!

songs.note: Qword’s solos didn’t fit on a phone screen in the app version. Fans kept pausing them with their thumbs.
songs.lesson: Touch is not a mouse. Fingers are imprecise and cover up whatever they touch, so touch targets need to be big (platform guidelines suggest roughly 44 to 48 points) and spaced apart, with feedback shown around the finger. There’s no hover on a touchscreen. Gestures like swipe, pinch and long press are invisible, so they need cues before people will discover them.

songs.title: Battery Low

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The screen’s the hungriest thing in the room,
The radio’s next, and the GPS will bring the doom.
Wake the phone up every second and it never gets to sleep,
And by lunchtime the battery is dead and buried deep!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Battery low! (Twenty percent!)
Battery low! (Ten percent!)
Do the work in batches and let the radio rest,
Battery low, battery low, and the sleeping phone is best!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Ask for location rarely, only when it’s really there,
Group the network calls together, and don’t wake up for air.
Work offline when the signal’s gone and sync when it comes back,
Every little bit you save keeps the user on track!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Screen! (Dim it!) Radio! (Batch it!)
GPS! (Sparingly!) Sleep! (Let it!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes starts with a busy fill and gets sparser bar by bar, as if he’s running out of power, until he’s hitting one drum every other bar. Then he rests completely for two bars, recharges, and comes back at full strength.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Battery low! (Twenty percent!)
Battery low! (Ten percent!)
Do the work in batches and let the radio rest,
Battery low, battery low, and the sleeping phone is best!

songs.note: The first version of the app kept the GPS on to show the nearest record store. It drained a full battery in an hour.
songs.lesson: Phones run on batteries, so energy is a real limit. The screen, the cellular and Wi-Fi radios and the GPS use the most power, and waking the phone up constantly stops it from ever sleeping deeply. Good apps batch their network requests, ask for location sparingly, work offline and sync later, and let the phone sleep.

songs.title: Game Loop

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Read the input, update the world, and draw it on the screen,
Then do it all again, sixty times a second, clean.
The loop never stops while the game is still alive,
Input, update, render, and the players come alive!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Game loop! (Input!)
Game loop! (Update!)
Game loop! (Render!)
Around and around, and never late!
Fast machine or slow machine, the game must feel the same,
Game loop, game loop, the heartbeat of the game!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Measure how much time went by and move things by that much,
Delta time, so the speed of the machine won’t change the touch.
Or step the physics at a fixed rate, steady as a clock,
And render when you’re able, and the world will never stop!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Delta time! (How long since the last?)
Fixed step! (Steady, not too fast!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s solo loops one phrase while Bytes speeds the beat up and slows it down underneath. Qword adjusts every note by how much time has passed, so the melody moves at exactly the same speed no matter how fast the loop goes.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Game loop! (Input!)
Game loop! (Update!)
Game loop! (Render!)
Around and around, and never late!
Fast machine or slow machine, the game must feel the same,
Game loop, game loop, the heartbeat of the game!

songs.note: A sequel to Sixty Frames from 2004. Wyrd built a game into the album app: catch the duck.
songs.lesson: Games run in a game loop: read the player’s input, update the game world (physics, enemies, scores), render the frame, and repeat, typically 30 to 60 or more times a second. Moving things by delta time, the time since the last frame, keeps the game the same speed on fast and slow machines. Many engines run physics at a fixed timestep for stability and render as often as they can.

songs.title: Entity Component System

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Back in eighty-five we built a family tree,
A dragon is a beast, and a beast’s a thing, you see.
But a flying, swimming, burning dragon broke the tree in two,
So throw away the family and compose something new!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Entity! (Just an ID!)
Component! (Just the data!)
System! (Does the work for every one that has the parts!)
Entity, component, system, that’s where the game starts!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: An entity’s a number with nothing else inside,
Components are the data, the position, health and size.
A system runs on every entity that has the parts it needs,
Movement moves the ones with velocity at the speed it reads!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Composition! (Over inheritance!)
Packed in arrays! (For cache-friendly speed!)
Add a component! (New behavior, indeed!)

parts.label: Snap-on parts: full band
parts.desc: The solo starts as a bare pulse, an entity with nothing attached. Then the band snaps on parts one at a time, bass, then guitar, then synth, each adding a behavior, and takes them off again in a different order. The groove changes every time, and nothing breaks.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Entity! (Just an ID!)
Component! (Just the data!)
System! (Does the work for every one that has the parts!)
Entity, component, system, that’s where the game starts!

songs.note: In the app’s game, Null was an entity with a position, a sprite and a velocity, but no sound component. Nobody added one. Nobody needed to.
songs.lesson: An entity component system (ECS) is an architecture common in game engines. Entities are just ID numbers. Components are plain data attached to them, like position, velocity or health. Systems run the logic over every entity that has the components they need, so a movement system moves everything with a position and a velocity. It favors composition over deep inheritance trees, and storing components in tightly packed arrays makes it fast.

songs.title: Embedded

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: No screen, no keyboard, just a chip inside the wall,
Sixty-four kilobytes, and it has to do it all.
It reads the temperature, it turns the motor on,
It runs for years on a battery, and it’s running when you’re gone!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Embedded! (Hidden inside!)
Embedded! (Nowhere to hide!)
Small memory, slow clock, and a deadline it must meet,
Embedded, embedded, in the toaster and the street!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Sensors read the world outside and actuators push it back,
An interrupt when something happens keeps it on the track.
The brakes must fire on time, not late, or someone could get hurt,
Real time means on time, not just fast, so stay alert!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Sense! (Read!) Decide! (Think!)
Act! (Move!) Before you blink!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo is allowed only four notes and must hit each one on an exact beat, never early, never late. It’s the smallest solo on the album and the hardest to play.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Embedded! (Hidden inside!)
Embedded! (Nowhere to hide!)
Small memory, slow clock, and a deadline it must meet,
Embedded, embedded, in the toaster and the street!

songs.note: Recorded on gear with less memory than the band’s first tape machine.
songs.lesson: Embedded systems are computers built into other things, like appliances, cars and sensors, often small microcontrollers with very little memory, low power and no full operating system. They read sensors, drive actuators like motors, and often respond to events with interrupts. Real-time systems must meet deadlines, and in hard real-time systems, like car brakes, a late answer is a wrong answer.

songs.title: Runs on the Fridge

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The lights are on the network and the doorbell has a brain,
The fridge is on the internet, and the milk has turned again.
A billion little devices, every one a tiny node,
Sensing and reporting from your kitchen to the road!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Runs on the fridge! (Open the door!)
Runs on the fridge! (Play it once more!)
Every device a platform, every object on the net,
Runs on the fridge, and we’re not finished yet!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: But every device online is another door to guard,
Update the firmware, change the passwords, and it shouldn’t be that hard.
Remember ninety-eight, the duck, the backstage pass,
The fridge is a computer now, so lock it up at last!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Web! (Phone!) Game! (Chip!)
Fridge! (Open the door!) And let the album rip!

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays the album’s biggest synth hook through the fridge’s tiny speaker, recorded straight off the door. It sounds terrible. The fans love it. Then the full band comes back in at full size.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Runs on the fridge! (Open the door!)
Runs on the fridge! (Play it once more!)
Every device a platform, every object on the net,
Runs on the fridge, and we’re not finished yet!

songs.note: Wyrd made a version of the album that runs on a smart fridge. It plays when you open the door. It is the most-played version.
songs.lesson: The Internet of Things connects everyday objects, like thermostats, lights, doorbells and appliances, to the network, each one a small embedded computer sensing and reporting. Every connected device is also a way in for attackers, so these devices need secure defaults, a unique password each, and firmware that can be updated.
